Can you have a smartphone without it being under surveillance by the CIA?

Not really. Here is why smartphone security and privacy is a pipe dream:

Cellular Radio

At the very least, phones with a cellular radio can have their location tracked regardless of what operating system you install on the phone, because much of the time it is a closed-source, proprietary chip that controls the radio. In some cases we don't know for sure that they are capable of anything malicious, but we also have no idea what they are or are not capable of. In any case, it's a black box outside of your control, that talks to cell towers that can triangulate.

In some devices (pdf) - admittedly this was a car- failure to isolate the cell radio chip from the main computer has allowed control of the main computer over the cell network. The example I linked is by no means the most recent, the most sophisticated, the newest, nor the only such attack -but it is one that I remember where the exploit to control the car's computer was because the cell radio in the car was improperly isolated.

The OS

Android is a mess security-wise, as is most consumer software. This is a design & use problem with the software that any android derivative is likely to suffer from. You could find an open-source, security-focused android derivative and decide if you trust them...

But you need the domain expertise to audit every line of their source code, because you don't know if the producers have been suborned by an intelligence agency, and hit with a gag order that prevents them from telling you.

Okay, so if not android, then what? Your choices are basically the closed-source iPhone (and closed-source is a nonstarter for security and privacy), Windows phone (and we know that at least the CIA completely owns Microsoft products and the alphabet soup agencies have for years), the defunct Blackberry ( software that is no longer being maintained means that no existing vulnerabilities will ever be patched), or something incredibly niche like Firefox or Ubuntu phone.

The Apps

Any application with cloud storage or push notifications is another company that you have to trust with your data & privacy, another likely closed-source application that you have to trust to not be spying on you, and another closed-source application with potential vulnerabilities that could be used to own your phone. Nowadays, this is almost every useful non-phone-call application.

The Other Wireless

Okay, so you have manually removed the cell chip from your phone, you are running a security - focused version of Ubuntu OS, you've installed a minimal amount of apps, all of them open-source.

Do you want to be able to connect to the Internet? Your Wi-Fi chip is probably no safer than your cell chip except that its range is generally much less… But you pass by many many more Wi-Fi hotspots in your day (probably) than you do cell towers. Do you connect to any of them? You'd better trust the operator of that hotspot, the vendor of the network hardware involved, and the ISP that is providing them internet access.... Consumer / retail network hardware usually has proprietary operating systems and/or firmware that is rarely, if ever updated... And are frequently compromised.

And even if you are on a hotspot with unexploitable firmware, and a trustworthy ISP, and a trustworthy hotspot operator, you still have to trust every other device within Wi-Fi signal range of your phone, because they can detect the data that you are sending to the hotspot.

Also Bluetooth.

Other People's Phones

All of the effort securing your own device does no good, if you're sitting at a table with (or potentially, even across the room from) somebody whose phone is happily transmitting audio and video back to an alphabet soup agency. Maybe the agency won't be able to see what's on your phone screen, but they could still learn where you were, at what time of day, and maybe have audio and/or video of what you did there. Maybe video of your smartphone screen.

Conclusion

There are many handoffs of data and sources of software involved in a modern smartphone. It generally only takes one weak link to compromise the security and privacy of the user, and there are so very very very many links - many of them beyond the ability of the smartphone user to do anything about - that it is basically impossible for the average smartphone user to have a high degree of confidence in the security and privacy of their device.

Should you give up? No, you should still keep desiring security and privacy, but the industry needs to change before this is something that will be able to offer consumers. In the meantime, "assume compromise."
